You been eating up, buddy. You kind of up there now with your weight.

Oh, yes, he was. Yeah. Put it weight about 12 pounds.

Yeah, well I had one of, I made, let's see, we played that World Series 1919, and Lawrence Stewart, I lost my copy, and Lawrence Stewart, he gave me a little postcard thing, you know? Yeah.

And this fella, man, was half drunk and he'd come shooting through the hall. My daddy had rafters up there. We had Cleo, he got drowned on the 6-0. He got drowned down on the ship. He was a steamship man. And he had his base, got caught up in the ceiling, you know, with the rafters. And he was trying to say, get out the way, Dr. Dunn. Excuse me, go ahead and stand there. I said, where's Papa? Papa, right out almost to the lake. Yeah, he's trying to, almost to the lake. I said, I thought you were such a brave man. He said, no, but he's shooting, Rowling.
You want my history?
Yes, if you could tell us a little bit about your life, it'd be wonderful.

I was born in 18, 24, 18, 7 to 9, with my parents. And then I went to school at the age of 8 years old. And me and my sister went to school together. 76. My father died on his birthday day when 76 years old.
When did he die? Do you remember the date about? What year? November 25th. November 25th. November 25th.

1935. November 25th. 76. On the last part of his birthday. He died on his birthday. Mm-hmm.
That's strange. Did your father ever play in any dance bands, or did he just teach most of the time?

Ah, yeah. Did you play the bass with a bow?

Yes, with a bow. Three string bass. Three string. I think it was a G, D, and A spread. And he keep putting in the Killing Melody Black plan. That's the first book. Yeah, I helped Percy too. Percy was playing drums. You know he was playing trumpet? Yeah, he started on drums.

Yes, I remember. I never heard him on drums. Other people have told me that. They used to hear him on drums. Yeah, I used to get a little job, you know. Get a little work in the cinema. When did you stop playing, Mr. Humphrey? How late did you work on it?

I stopped playing clarinet at the 23-year-old. Frank Lewis taught me. He showed the keys. I was married at 23-year-old. I was married at 23-year-old. I was first to play music at the 19-year-old. I was first to play music at the 19-year-old.
Yeah, I finished here in 19-year-old. Yeah, I finished here in 19-year-old.
Mm-hmm. Wow.

No, I went, I taught, I taught bands in 1932, 1937.
There were some school bands. Yeah, I did.
Yeah.

Um, I played in 50 different, 50 different bands. I played in Los Angeles and we played Mr. McVeer and played, played banjo, three pieces. I used to do it. We played saxophone band, and band, and bass. The other day we met Mr. August Loran. He said he played in,

blocks.x: Who else was in the Silverleaf band who played trumpet?
I believe Mipolite Charles was playing the trumpet at the time. That's right. And Mr. Baptiste, Albert Baptiste was the leader. Who did he play? He played violin.
And the trombonist?

I think we, at the time I think we had Paul Benn. No, he was a boy from up the country there and he played around. We had Paul Benn and Jimmie Johnson was playing the bass in that band. And let's see, I can't think of some of those other guys. Oh yeah, I believe Lil' Kato was playing drums.
I think we had a big role in the band. After you finished the boat job, what did you do then?

Well, I went to Chicago. See, it had to go fair. I went to Chicago out of Davenport. That's where we finished our summer season. And I had to either come by the way of St. Louis or Chicago to come back home. So I went to Chicago. And the first night I got a job with George Fields. And T.O.A. had just ran away from those. They left over that band and they had an opening. So they asked a fellow named Fernandez. Used to play with Dave Peet and they helped play with them. You know, after the show at the Grand Heath come and play with them at the Deluxe at 35th and State. When I went in there so they gave me a chance. I had never played with none of those guys but they knew of me through my family, you see. And so they gave me a chance up there and I played with them. I did all right. Until Manuel or Freddie came from Chicago, from New York. And he was a pretty good mixer, you know, a little better than Manuel. He used to spend all his money so he got the job. So the place closed down for repairs and Freddie went in there. Well, he went there with Tony Jackson and Noah Dutre and my cousin was on the drum Tubby. And let's see, there was five of those. There was five pieces. So I went back with him, asked George to leave me off and I went back in the place with Freddie. He said, well, if I get a job will you come with me? So I gave him my award, you know. So when he got a job down in the loop, at the beginning of the loop, 22nd War Bash, well I put Freddie in there and went with George. But the job didn't last long. It was a Fryberg place. That's an old place there right by the L train, 22nd War Bash. But it didn't last long and I believe I made my mistake there. I should have stayed with Freddie.
The time you played there at the ballpark, that picture was...

Well that was when I was working with Manuel and them. And Joe and them, they were playing the Royal, no, Joe was playing Bill Bata's Dreamland. And we made up, well all the bands were invited through the fans, you know, they paid our way, it wasn't with the dollars that were going, they paid our way. But we made more than that, we picked up about thirty-something dollars a piece in the park.
Two million money, huh?

Yeah. Well that time it was plenty of money. Yeah, it was made up with George, George Fields, he played. And I came, I got sick, I came back home and I got back here, these fellas around here were making more money than they made in Chicago. Going up and down, right after the war then, you see. Going up and down the road to Hammond, Ponchatoula. And I joined up with Amos Riley, was in charge of the band. It was the Tulane band. And Frankie Dusen was playing in the band at the time. And I joined up and I did real well. And then we got a chance to go to Roof Garden, was played there. And then Frankie had in charge of the band, Frankie Dusen, I worked with him, I used to lead the band. And we went from the Pithin' Roof Garden to the Royal Garden in the winter, in the summer with the Pithin' Roof Garden. And after we put the top on it, well I was prepping this man there. In the meantime we had every Saturday night at Jones Country Club for a number of years. And I stayed with Frank a good while that I quit from the roof garden, a little something come up with it. And then I went to work at Tom's Roadhouse. And this boy Zutty, he's the one who gave me the job. He'd hit the drum and he had that overhead pedal and you hit it and it would bounce back a couple of times. You know, he didn't have to hang on to it. But he got to be a big time drummer after this. So when I left there, let's see what I'd do. Well I organized my own band I think. I had my Duran Humphrey and we did pretty well around there. We did pretty well around there. And so I quit my band. I quit, what did I do there? I quit, yeah that's what it is. I think I quit to go back on the boat. I don't know if I quit to go back on the boat, but I quit and I went back on the boat. I quit and I went on a regular job, that's what it was. Went on some kind of regular job, I don't know where it was now. But anyway, after that, let's see. Oh yeah, I worked with Kid Ren there. He was on a pledge for a year, not drinking. So I joined him and we did real well. And that's where I left and went back on the boat. That was in 1925. So I just went out there making, there was people so particular I knew them. Went out there just to make a nice work.
Which boat was at the capital?

It was the capital then, it was the capital. And I worked and we signed up, I went out of St. Louis, we had a real good band. I was under the direction of Dewey Jackson at the time. So Dewey I don't think came back, no he didn't come back I don't think. So fate took over the band. So I signed up again, every season we signed St. Louis for this, winter season, signed here for the summer. That's how we used to do it, two contracts a year.
Was it the other way around, summer up there?

Summer, yeah. Up in St. Louis, in the winter here. That's right. And so I worked off and on, I worked about twelve years for those people. I didn't know you were that long there on the boat. I played tenor sax.
Tenor sax most of the time.

Yeah, well you had to play that with the other three instruments you see. Of course I featured the clarinet. And so I left the boat, made a little trip and I came back home. Oh I think I was married then. And so Dewey, he had a little job, so he sent him, so I went to play with Dewey. Went back to St. Louis, stayed up there close to two years I believe. I had to come back home, to the loud a little bit. I worked with whoever, Larry. And we did pretty nice.
How long have you been teaching music now too?

Well I've been, I've been in this, let's say about, 1934, since 1934, 33 or 34. See when I came back from St. Louis, there was no work. Depression then. Depression, see I came back in 32. And I believe my, yeah my daddy was here. They went, we were, he was a fellow named Professor Turo. He was a fine musician. I don't know if anybody ever mentioned him, he's a fine musician around here. And through him and my, he and my daddy, while I got to work in the school, through this private school, see. And we had access to all the public schools. Little political stuff, you see, they did. And then I used to go and teach the different school bands in the afternoons. Because there's a lawyer, you can't teach in there until after, after three o'clock, you see. Yeah, for private people, you know. And we used to go in, I'd be at three o'clock, and at three to five, he did too. So we had access to all the schools. Your father taught them in the schools? He did, yeah, that's right. And, well, it didn't look like much, but do you know, you're parling nickels and dimes up, it sort of mounted something.
In those days, a lot of the musicians were in that WPA band.

Well, yeah, when I was in the band, I got in the band after that. After that, I had to do something. Any of your brothers in it too? No, no, none of them. I was the only one. And it looked like I wasn't going to be able to get in. They looked like they tried to keep me out of it a long time. Then that's when I left the WPA, and I got a call with the Millsboro Rhythm. And I worked around there, I guess, about six months.
Around New York, or where did you go?
Yeah, yeah, I went to New York. I went to Washington, D.C. I went to New York, and I made records, and a good bit of records, actually.
I might even have heard you in those days, and didn't know you were in the band. I didn't know who the musicians were. Yeah, yeah.

Nice to hear that. I made a trip out of New York, clean down through Texas. We had a package, played all the theaters, all the shows in Texas, all through Texas. Of course, San Antonio played. Went back, and the weather was kind of bad. We were supposed to go back in some place in Pennsylvania. We played, what's that, some theater in Pittsburgh we played. I can't forget the name of it.
Is it out on Wiley Avenue or downtown?
No, it's a big theater downtown. Downtown. I can't think of it. I can't think of it.
The one that had the good bands, I heard Tats Waller out of it.

Well, it must be the bands where all the bands go. We had a package. We had a real good show. We had Pops and, we had Stanley. Stanley, that's what, yeah, Stanley. Pops and Lloyd, we had, we had these two comedians, they were very good. Bud Williams or Bud something, and Boyd, Bud and Boyd I believe they called themselves. And they were good. Remember Bucking Bubbles? No, no, it wasn't Bucking Bubbles. We had this girl, this woman here, some Wilson. She was a singer. Edith Wilson? Edith Wilson was on with us. You heard talk about it. Yeah, I never heard, she made records, never heard of her. Yeah, well she was on a package with us. When I came back, when I come back, well then I just started working short bands, you see. I worked with, well time to time I worked with different bands, I played with Pierron, you know. All the bands I substitute, not regular, because they wanted me to Tuxedo bands a long time but I never would join them regular, original Tuxedos. And I played with the Excelsior band, the old Excelsior band, a long time. Until I started going away on the boat, you see, well that disrupted, you see. And after that, well I didn't bother, I was out of the band, see, and got somebody else.
You really liked the brass band?
The brass band, yeah.
I used to play a lot of fumes and parades. Did you ever play E-flat there and everything? Yeah, I got two E-flats home, I didn't have a condition. That's when I played E-flat. E-flat and everything?
Yeah, I never played B-flat.

I just used this and this and condition, you see. They had music and everything for it. And it was a music band. They didn't do much. They played a little by head but most of them music, marches and all that stuff, they had heavy funerals, you tell you. They had a real number one band for eleven pieces. We could have used a little more complemented entry. We just used one peckhorn, see, but we could have used another to bounce a little more. We used a baton, bass and a peckhorn, you see. And they'd have three trombones, I mean two trombones and two drums and three trumpets.
Some of the bands used two alto peckhorns then? Sometimes or not?

I don't remember none of them using two but they should have had two. It's good to have a crew. Yeah, it would have been nice if they could have used twelve, you know men? Yeah. And they had used two peckhorns to give that and a complement. It would be much better. When your grandmothers... Of course, I'll tell you another thing though, you know trombones, they give you a complement too on marches, few marches and things like that. So it's done pretty nice there. Because they used to write the parts that used to say first and second tenor, you see. And they'd give them two horns if they'd split the parts up. It'd come out nice because they used to write band music that way, huh?
You mean they'd play first and second parts?

Yeah, yeah. Well the trumpets used to have two solos and the first would be flat. Well naturally they would harmonize, you see, when one's up to, you know what I mean, two at the time. And the trombones, they used to have first and second tenors. Well the trombones could play that part, you see. I think it sounded pretty good when everybody was playing. For the eleven men, the bands used to do pretty good. And the Reading the Tuxedo band was pretty nice too. They used to play a lot of music.
I was wondering about the bands your grandfather had, the brass bands he taught, did they ever really play much jazz or were they just strictly the music that was printed there?

Well I don't think they, I really don't know it would be truthful. I wondered if you heard them when you were a boy. No, I don't. What they were like. I don't, but I do know he used to bring his country boys down here to play them big mardi gras. Did they do big parades? I heard about that too.
Yeah.

And he used to play them. My granddad used to play them. Harrison Barnes told us about that. I remember him saying that they'd meet at these parades that start at the canal and the river. And I remember him saying that it would be so cold sometimes that the valves would freeze. It would freeze on the horns and water would get watered in them. I remember him saying that.
And he already played the St. Patrick's Day parade.
They had big parades on St. Patrick's Day then too.
On the 17th, yeah, the show day. 17th, that was March of New. March 17th.
March 17th. That's the little St. Patrick. Oh that's right. I haven't heard anything about it down here. In New York they have a big Irish parade. Was it 14th?
I said it was the little St. Patrick.
14th, eh? Yeah. 17th.
17th.
17th, that's right. They haven't had it yet.
No, it's Tuesday. 17th.
Haven't had it yet. How did they get all the banter because of that?
17th. Well if Perry Como, he had a program, he had a program, and he had a line.
St. Patrick's Zone. It was last night. Oh, that's right there. And all St. Perry's Zone. They don't do any of that St. Patrick's Day parading now on New Orleans.
Not here, no. They used to. They used to have it.
They do do.

But they're trying to play up all that stuff now. Like they're trying to lure tourists here, I noticed in the people. They're trying to get some sort of program. And I saw it today, where they're going to try and have some kind of big hotel. Well they plan on going to hotel on the late front. Anyway. They're going to have activities and things out there. I don't know. Well, you got to spend money to make it.

I was wondering, Will, if you have a couple minutes to talk yet about your brother Earl. I've never met him. I hope we'll get to talk to him someday. But in case we don't for a while, if you could. Was he older, younger than you? No, Earl's next to me. Just about two years younger.
You're the oldest. You haven't worked there in September.
How old would he be in September, Earl? He'd be 56, I'd say he was. Yeah.

Or 50. No, in September he'd be 57, because I'd be 59 at these times. So he'd be close by two years or less. Did he start right on the trombone? No, he started on his shell. And he, by granddaddy, should write bass parts for him, you know. But he was smaller. Yeah. And then he, when he got here, he started playing the bass. And he had a trombone. I still got the trombone over there. I put it in condition. Old York trombone. And he started, my granddaddy started teaching him the trombone. And first thing you know, he was out here playing. Yeah. And he was out here playing. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. He still plays bass. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah.
He still plays bass. Well, yeah, but I don't know.
He still plays bass. Somebody said they heard him over there in Virginia.

But they don't play bass. Yeah. He was playing. He was playing around. He stopped playing the trombone. He didn't have no instruments to practice on. So, he started playing around here at these different bands and he worked this Jitney business. He worked under one of these Jitneys down there a long time. It was the first real job I think was when my daddy took him off on the circus and he worked with me in California. And, uh, when he came back, well, he went on the circus. He worked with Salesforce too. He used to be on the corner. He'd been all up the counter. He traveled much more than my daddy on that counter. Then he, I believe my dad took him out on a minstrel show. What minstrel is that you're on, Papa? My dad's a minstrel man too, you know.
He's playing minstrel. He was on the minstrel.

What's the name of that minstrel he was on? Old Man Quine show. It wasn't a rabbit foot. What was the other one? Old Man Quine show. What's the other show? Rabbit was owned by Quine. They had the rabbit foot and they had another show. I just remember. I just remember. I just remember. Oh, it was on a show. It wasn't a rabbit foot. It's, uh, it's operated by the same people. Oh, I used to kid all the time about that show. I can't think of it. But anyhow, he traveled minstrel shows.
Several of them called Georgia. No, it wasn't Georgia Minstrel.

No, it wasn't that, no. No, they had a whole lot of musicians traveling in Georgia, but if you tell me they had a fine band, they did. I remember Georgia Minstrel. Yeah. John Porter was in there, and I think, and, uh, Charlie McCurdy, and, uh, David Jones, he was quite young. He made all of that. No, after he traveled around, he worked with Chris Kelly around here a long time, and he played those jitney dances. That's about all I knew he played with. Yeah, well that was. On the roof over the minor. That's right, he played on the roof over the minor. That's right, he sure did.

You were in that band of Ireland, too, weren't you fast on that? Well, I was on them, I used to play up there. I believe Johnny St. Cyr was in that band. Yeah. I have a picture with you in that band, too. That's right, I was in that. The first night they put the roof over it. They took a picture with a doctor's dance. See, I'll get a copy of that for you sometime.
Yeah, I'd like to see that.
The band's so small, you can hardly see who's in it, but Johnny told me he'd play it out.
Yeah, well we used to work together. Yeah. It was a long time.
Yeah.
We worked with Frankie Duesen a long time. Frank played in the band together with Frankie.
How was Frankie in those days? Was he pretty rough, or was he smooth playing, or how was he doing?
Rough. Rough as they made him. Really? We had a father now, he would've. He begged me, begged me to come back with him, but I never would go back and play with him. Was he rough?
Was he a fly?
Oh yeah, you know he was fly. Frankie Duesen was a chur.
Where's he from?

Frankie Duesen told me at the time they played at the old Paris Prism and he was playing the valve I believe, I don't know if it was valve or slide, I don't know what it was, but anyway, one of them keepers broke his horn, or somebody broke his horn. Broke Frank his horn, yeah. Yeah. So he said, I'm sorry, I don't worry about it, I'll buy you another. So Frank was kind of glad, you know. So he made him go to the oil lines, or glue walls, I believe it was. And the old man that was the clerk there, and his man met him. So the horns were cheaper than what they are now, but the man thought he'd get him a horn for about $10 to $15, you know. So Frank picked out the best horn. The man told him about $35 or $40, $50. He said, what, for what? He said, I wouldn't pay that for Gable's horn.
That's why he's got a Gable.

That's like we played the Boston club, one was New Year's Eve night, and one of them big guys come, the only ship, the ship line out there, he came in the club and he had something wrapped up which was liquor in a bottle, see. And he come in, he was all stewed up. And he came over to the band and said, I say, stop that music. Well we looked at him, so Frank, he's, I don't pay him no mind. So he kept on, I say, stop that music. That music sounds like hell to me when I'm drunk. Stop that music. And he got right near the bass player, Alex Scott was playing the bass, and he took that bottle and he hit that bass in the side and burst that bass. So Frank said, don't worry about it, we'll talk to the president. So that John M. Parker's brother was president then, see. He said, we'll take care of it. We'll see that he'll pay you for it. So he come back and he gave him, offered for Alec $10. Well Alec was the fellow who could fix up that bass, you know, patch it up. So Alec wanted to take the 10, Frank wouldn't let him take it. He said, you can't get no bass for that, you got to get you a new bass. So he come back, offered him $20. Alec wanted that. He kept on, raised the $10 and $5 like that, and Frank kept telling him, he said, don't take it. He said, I ain't going to give you nothing. So Alec was saying, now look there, Frank, you can fix it so I'm going to even get my money for my bass. So I can take this bass and fix it up and start playing, keep playing. But sure enough, I believe the band accepted $50 at $60. So Alec passed the bass up at that night to see Alec somebody robbed him of that money. He got drunk and he threw up all that money. He wasn't there, but that's right. That's right.
That's a shame.
That's about all I know about where he played on the shores. He'd be at carnivals, you know, and circuses.
I hope he gets over here soon and I'd like to meet him.

Well, I'm pretty sure he'll be drifting around. He'll be here soon. He usually come around every once in a while, you know, every once, every two years he'd come down, something like that. So it's about time for him to come in.
It'd be nice to get his voice on the tape too, talking about the old days and that.

One night over at the Dream Room you were telling me about several old musicians, old time musicians. I remember saying I'd never heard of them before. I can't remember now who the names were even, but they said you remembered way back some of those... Oh, Gus Madcalf, I don't know if you... No, don't know about him. Oh, Gus, yeah, I don't know Gus.
I remember Lewis Dumain.
I remember Lewis Dumain, yeah. Did you play with him too?
Yeah, I played with him. He had sort of... He was some kind of director in the WP band.
Oh, your brother made some records with him too, I believe.
Oh, that's right. The Red Onion Drag. And this Ann Cookie here I'm talking about. Oh, yeah, that's right. He made something. He certainly did.
Gus Madcalf, what did he play?
He played, I'll tell you, not my granddaddy taught him. He played trombone. He used to play a biotone and peck horn. That's right. He was pretty good.
That was Bob's cousin. Yeah, that's right.
Bob Lyons' cousin.
Oh, Bob Lyons' cousin. That's the best.

Oh, we had a whole lot of musicians around here. We had a follow-up, he used to play... Johnny Browns? Johnny Browns would play violin. And he played clarinet after? Yeah. And you don't remember Stanley, do you? He used to play trombone for him?
Well, he used to talk about Joe Johnson.
I don't know if everybody ever mentioned about Joe Johnson. Joe Johnson. He's a trumpet player.
I've heard of him, don't know much about him. He played on front of him. No.
Well I didn't know, I hear him talk about it. My cousin used to play with him, he's from Carlton. Yeah, Joe, I saw a trumpet player.
And I see him talking about a trumpet player called Ned.
What was his name, Ned what? He used to play with Ned.
He used to play with Ned.
He used to play with Ned.

He used to play with Ned. He used to play with Ned. He used to play with Ned. He used to play with Ned. He was like a little mule on the face. Ned, yeah. He was like a little mule. Like a little jackass. Had a strong lip. Yeah, you knew him, man. I knew his son. I met his first class musician.
He was? Yeah, he was so Ned. He played with Buddy too.
He did? He played with Buddy Ball then too.
Yeah, Buddy Johnson.
I know you got to do that by Buddy Johnson and Jack. Yeah, he was strong. Do you know Ned's name, is that his last name? P-V-D-Q Ned. I think that is right. P-V-D-Q Ned. What?
See what? P-V-D-Q Ned. P-V-D-Q Ned. P-V-D-Q Ned.
P-V-D-Q Ned. P-V-D-Q Ned.
P-V-D-Q Ned. P-V-D-Q Ned. P-V-D-Q Ned. P-V-D-Q Ned. P-V-D-Q Ned. P-V-D-Q Ned. P-V-D-Q Ned.

P-V-D-Q Ned. P-V-D-Q Ned. P-V-D-Q Ned. P-V-D-Q Ned. P-V-D-Q Ned. P-V-D-Q Ned. He called himself P-V-D-Q Ned. Oh, that's what he called himself. I think that was his... I think... I don't know if... I knew his boy. I don't remember my name Ned. Yeah.

Maybe Ned was his last name. I think it was. I think it was. Because he had a boy working at the Klobel and Derrick. When I was in the saloon business, he used to come in there and I used to give him credit. I can't remember the name.
You know John Pendleton, didn't you?
No, I heard talk about him.
Well, you know John Pendleton. Yes. John Pendleton. He used to play trombone. Trumpe. He used to play trumpe?
Yes. There's a whole lot of like... I speak like two-row. Two-row was a... You know old man Claymore Williams? You getting any information on him at all?
Yes, we've heard people up at Donaldsonville.
Yeah, and his brother... Tell me his brother was one of the greatest biotone players. It was George. George, that's right.
He played trombone too, didn't he?

I think he was a biotone. But he was... No honest... But I... Did he play trombone too? I didn't know. He played trombone. I think somebody told me... But I know he was one of the... They said he was one of the greatest biotone players. He was. Zilp had a miss. And you didn't meet... You all didn't get in touch with David Jones in California. No, we missed him.
We tried to find him.
And you couldn't find Wade Willie, you say? No.
I'm afraid Wade is dead maybe, but Jones is still out there. I know, Ed.
He was there when I was there. He was doing... He was a maintainer's man in some place. He moved...
He moved a couple of times, and I couldn't get his address until about the last day I was there. And then he didn't have a phone.
No, can't go further back, Papa. He was the wall itching.
Well, we must run along in a couple of minutes.
Well, you got Amos Roddy, I know you. Yes, we had a nice... And uh... Alex Scott. Amos Roddy.
Wait, we didn't see Amos Roddy. Amos Roddy. He was a trumpet player.
Yeah, trumpet player. He had the two-lane band, the brass band. All the dog fellas. And his nephew, Alex Scott. He was a very good bass player. Very good. Very good.
Alex used to play with me. Alex used to play with me.
I knew you didn't talk about Jimmy Pauline. Oh, yes. Yes. And Spencer. Wow.
David used to play with Tronman. Yeah. Nox at Butts.
Well, that's a hit of mine. I know nothing about him. John McCullough at the Browns, you should know. Yeah, I don't remember. Are you supposed to play with Tronman?
Yeah. I don't remember. Are you supposed to play with him?
Yeah, I don't remember. Are you supposed to play with him?
New York, how are you supposed to play with Tronman?
Mm-hmm. I used to play with Tronman.

Oh, yeah. Eddie Jackson. I played with his band, too. The Nola band. The Nola band. Yeah. The Nola band. I played with the Nola band. You remember that. You played. You played with the band. Yeah. Eddie Jackson, Peter La Caz. And who had, I don't know what was it, Paul's band? Or, what? Heisenbaum. Heisenbaum.
Heisenbaum.

Heisenbaum. Heisenbaum. Oh, we had a whole lot of musicians around there. Oh, yeah. There were so many. Yeah, you'd remember. You'd be writing a long time. Every once in a while, I'd think about some new ones.
Yeah, yeah, yeah. Anybody know what time it is? Steve. Steve Lewis. You know if you heard about Steve? The piano player, yeah. Yeah. Huh? Ten after four.
I got ten after four. Ten after four. It must be later than that. We didn't.
Oh, it has to be later than that, Fess. I don't know if I'm wondering why I'm watching.

It has to be later than that because we didn't get here until a little after three and we've been... Oh, yes, after four. We've been talking almost an hour and a half here. I enjoy it every bit too. So it must be five o'clock. We must run along. Oh. Let this tape run on through here for a minute and we'll get ready to go. Yeah, Willi remember.
Well, Willi was way behind me though, you know. Oh, yeah. Little Willi. Sure, little. I was a big Willi.
He's got ten years on you though. It's ten after five. This is my uncle. That's my aunt's husband.
How do you do? Good to know you. I'm Mr. Monetta, Professor Monetta, Mr. Thompson. All right, Mr. Thompson.
You met Mr. Russell. I believe he was able to do Mr. Thompson. Mr. Collins. How do you do? How do you do? Please meet Mr. Thompson.
How do you do?
All right.
Did you ever play any music Mr. Thompson? Quite a little. Banjo. Oh, banjo.
Or guitar.
Or guitar. Yeah. Oh, my way we used to have a quartet.
Six boys. We used to sing on the fire. It sounds so good on the river. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
